newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Germany averts petrol tax rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Germany averts petrol tax rise.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition avoided the political pitfall of raising petrol taxes but only at the cost of delaying a planned cut in the unpopular solidarity surcharge, officials said on Friday.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel said there was little room to cut spending further to bridge a 1997 budget gap that widened suddenly this week after a standoff with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) over his proposed tax bill.
But German taxpayers made clear they would hold the coalition to its promises to lower taxes.

Waigel told a news conference the tax changes would not jeopardise the government's goal of reducing its deficit to 2.5 percent of economic output in 1997, comfortably below the 3.0 percent required to join the single European currency at the scheduled start in 1999.
"We will have no higher deficit," Waigel said.
He said the delay in cutting the solidarity surcharge would bring about 3.7 billion marks ($2.4 billion) to government coffers.
That is nearly enough to offset the four billion marks lost by an accelerated increase in government child benefits, decided by default this week in the deadlock with the SPD.
A further three billion marks in spending cuts will need to be found in 1997, but the government will seek to spare investment outlays from the austerity pressures, Waigel said.
SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine said the decision not to cut the solidarity surcharge in January 1997 showed the government's tax policy was out of control.
"State finances are so far off course that the government now has to take away tax cuts it promised only yesterday," Lafontaine said.

Kohl's junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), who have made a name with anti-tax slogans, tried to put the best face on the matter by stressing that the bargain hammered out by coalition leaders on Friday included no tax increases.

Instead, the government agreed not reduce the solidarity tax -- imposed to help finance the reconstruction of formerly communist east Germany -- which was to have been cut to 6.5 percent from the current 7.5 percent from January 1.
The German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), a think tank with close ties to the SPD and unions, said the delay would hurt economic growth.
DIW economist Dieter Vesper said the government should halve the solidarity tax in 1997, raise the petroleum tax, and live with a higher deficit that would help stimulate the economy.
"In an upturn the deficit will automatically shrink," Vesper said.
Reports this week that the government was considering an increase in the petroleum tax sparked widespread protest from opposition parties, business associations and taxpayer groups.

The conservative daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung said despite pressure to bring Germany's budget in line with the Maastricht criteria for the single European currency, raising taxes was the wrong way to go.
Germans are better prepared to tolerate more government austerity than to pay ever higher taxes, the newspaper said. "There has to be an end to this now," it said in an editorial.
The government had considered raising the petroleum tax by 10 pfennigs a litre -- a measure which could have boosted revenues by an estimated seven billion marks.
The Taxpayers' Alliance strongly opposed the move.
"Citizens and enterprises are already suffering under an excessive burden of taxes and other withholdings," the alliance said in a statement.
Further reductions should be made in subsidies to east Germany and government personnel costs so taxes do not need to be raised, the alliance said.
